page.h1: HTS Chapter 76: Aluminum and Articles Thereof — Export Markets & Foreign Tariffs on U.S. Goods

seo.title: Tariffs on U.S. Aluminum & Scrap by Country (HTS Ch. 76) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What Canada, Mexico, China, the EU, India, Thailand, Malaysia, Korea and Hong Kong charge on U.S. aluminum and scrap: Canada's 50% surtax, China's 35% on scrap, and each buyer's import rules.
keywords: tariff on us aluminum scrap china

intro: Tariffs on U.S. aluminum split three ways. **Scrap**, a third of the chapter, enters Thailand, Malaysia, South Korea and Hong Kong duty-free and India at 2.5–5%, so what decides access is the buyer's purity, inspection and permit rules (see each market's regulator) — except in **China**, where U.S. scrap that meets its recycled-aluminum standards pays **35%** and scrap that does not is banned as solid waste. **Finished aluminum** enters Mexico, Korea and, since July 1, 2026, the EU free when it qualifies, but **Canada** adds a **50% surtax** on U.S. ingot, extrusions, sheet, foil and most articles, Mexico charges US$1.72/kg anti-dumping duty on U.S. hollow profiles, and Malaysia charges 25–30% on most semi-finished products.
valueBasis: FOB value of U.S. exports, as reported by the United States to UN Comtrade.

profile.headline: Mexico is the largest market ($3.83B, down 7.9%), mostly sheet and plate (7606, $950M), unwrought aluminum (7601, $680M) and other articles (7616, $547M). Qualifying goods enter free under USMCA, but U.S. hollow profiles (7604.21) have paid a US$1.72/kg anti-dumping duty since September 2026, and goods that fail the rule of origin now face general rates of 25–35% on many extrusion, sheet, tube and article lines.

profile.headline: Canada ($3.03B, down 5.5%) buys mainly sheet and plate (7606, $944M), cans and containers (7612, $606M) and unwrought aluminum (7601, $277M). Ingot, extrusions, sheet, foil and most articles have paid a Canadian surtax since March 13, 2025 — 25% at first, 50% since September 8, 2026 — even when they qualify for CUSMA. Scrap, powders, cans and gas cylinders are not on the list, and aluminum for Canadian manufacturing or food and beverage packaging can have the surtax remitted if imported before July 1, 2027.
profile.mainProducts: Plates, sheets and strip (over 0.2 mm) (7606) · Casks, drums, cans and boxes (up to 300 l) (7612)
profile.tariffNow: Free (CUSMA) + 50% surtax on most aluminum (not scrap or cans)

profile.headline: Thailand ($1.02B, up 34.8%) is almost all scrap: 96% is aluminum scrap (7602, $981M), and scrap enters duty-free. Since October 2026 Thai Customs unloads and inspects every container declared as metal scrap, and the government has proposed limiting scrap imports to licensed factories with pre-shipment inspection, so clean, accurately declared loads matter.
profile.mainProducts: Aluminum waste and scrap (7602) · Aluminum powders and flakes (7603)
profile.tariffNow: Free on scrap; 3–10% MFN on aluminum products

regulator.name: Thai Customs Department (metal-scrap inspection)
regulator.requirement: Metal scrap can still be imported, but every container declared as scrap is physically unloaded and inspected, e-waste found inside is prohibited, and offending loads are sent back at the importer's cost (Customs press release 5/2570, October 21, 2026). A ban with licensed-factory imports and pre-shipment inspection has been proposed but not adopted

profile.headline: India ($853M, up 7.7%) is mainly a scrap market (7602, $787M), and scrap pays 2.5–5% basic customs duty. U.S. scrap cleared at one of eight listed ports (Chennai, Tuticorin, Kandla, JNPT, Mumbai, Krishnapatnam, Mundra and Kattupalli) needs no pre-shipment inspection certificate, only a supplier certificate. India told the WTO in 2025 that it might retaliate for U.S. aluminum tariffs but has applied nothing.
profile.mainProducts: Aluminum waste and scrap (7602) · Plates, sheets and strip (over 0.2 mm) (7606)

regulator.name: Directorate General of Foreign Trade (scrap import conditions and NFMIMS registration)
regulator.requirement: Aluminum scrap follows Handbook of Procedures para 2.51: shredded scrap needs a pre-shipment inspection certificate for radiation, unshredded scrap enters only at designated ports, and U.S. scrap at the eight listed ports needs only a supplier certificate. Importers of listed aluminum items must also register in the Non-Ferrous Metal Import Monitoring System (NFMIMS) before customs clearance

assumptions: Rates are what U.S.-origin goods pay in November 2026. Each column uses one representative six-digit subheading, the one with the largest 2025 U.S. exports in that heading (for example 7602.00 for scrap, 7606.12 for alloy sheet, 7607.11 for foil and 7612.90 for cans). Where a national 2026 schedule or decree was checked (Canada's CBSA tariff, EU TARIC, Mexico's decrees, China's 2026 provisional rates, Malaysia's April 2025 base rates) it is used; otherwise the rate is the World Bank/UNCTAD WITS (TRAINS) MFN applied rate for 2023, the latest year WITS holds. National 8–10-digit lines can differ.

Mexico, Canada and Korea show the FTA rate for qualifying goods. USMCA's Chapter 76 rules (Annex 4-B) mostly require a change of heading: sheet (7606) rolled from imported ingot qualifies, wire (7605) drawn from imported rod does not. Mexico's normal-rate column shows the general rates set by the decrees of December 29, 2025 and April 23, 2026.

Canada's cells add the surtax of the United States Surtax Order (Steel and Aluminum 2025): 50% on the 27 tariff items in its Schedule 1.1 and 25% on household articles (7615). The remission available for aluminum used in Canadian manufacturing, packaging or vehicles, and for listed products and importers, is on Export rules.

China's cells add, in order, China's MFN or 2026 provisional rate, the counter-tariff the line carries (25% on scrap under China's 2018 response to Section 232; 10–25% on other lines under its 2019 lists answering Section 301), and the 10% extra duty on all U.S. goods. An importer holding an exclusion from the 2019 counter-tariffs (valid to December 31, 2026) pays less; scrap has no exclusion route.
The EU cells show the 0% that Regulation (EU) 2026/1455 grants U.S. goods from July 1, 2026, with the conventional duty that applied before (and still applies to other origins) as the normal rate.
Only border duties are shown. India's surcharges on top of basic customs duty, VAT, GST and other internal taxes are the buyer's business and are left out.
